summary:
Same-sex conduct has been lawful in Croatia since 1977, and transgender people may serve openly in the armed forces. Hate-crime legislation enumerates both sexual orientation and gender identity. The age of consent was equalised at 14 in 1998 and raised to 15 by the Penal Code that took effect on 1 January 2013.

Enforcement lags the statute book. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report records that minority representatives describe anti-discrimination provisions covering employment, housing, education and health as inconsistently enforced, that NGOs report uneven judicial handling of discrimination cases and limited access to justice, and that victims are reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and of being victimised during trial. Hate-crime investigations are flagged as inadequate.

A 2018 Zagreb Pride documentation report on Croatia's implementation of Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 covers hate-crime legislation and the under-reporting of homophobic and transphobic crimes, hate-speech case studies, freedom of assembly, legal gender recognition, same-sex partnership recognition, employment discrimination, and compiled hate-crime data with case studies.

Croatian law since a 2013 legislative amendment permits registration of a changed gender marker without alteration of sex characteristics. A 2026 Croatian legal journal article analyses how police, customs and court officers must conduct searches of trans and gender-nonconforming persons under the Criminal Procedure Act, Police Powers Act, Customs Act and prison-sentences law, working through case studies of search difficulties and documenting the post-2013 framework in practice.

The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025, covering 2024, records that a Zadar prosecutor charged a man for refusing a gay couple's accommodation booking (2018 incident); that anti-gender disinformation is escalating, with a Croatian Parliament session on 'Gender Ideology' featuring speakers spreading misinformation and no LGBTI organisations invited; and that the first Pula Pride march faced disruption the day before.

Life partnerships have been available since 2014, following a 2013 constitutional referendum that banned same-sex marriage. Full same-sex adoption rights date from a 2022 final court ruling; the Constitutional Court ruled on 7 February 2020 that excluding same-sex couples from foster care was unconstitutional and discriminatory, and Mladen Kožić and Ivo Šegota became Croatia's first same-sex foster parents in September 2020 after a three-year legal battle. As of January 2024 no national statute regulates same-sex adoption, protections resting on court rulings alone. The Center for Social Welfare had initially rejected their application twice.

Article 68 of the Life Partnership Act grants life partners the same health insurance and healthcare rights as married heterosexual couples and prohibits adverse treatment of life partnerships in those areas. Reproductive care remains unequal: the Medically Supported Fertilization Law limits IVF to married heterosexual couples and single infertile women, excluding same-sex couples; a 2012 law had allowed single women but not lesbian couples. In 2023 the opposition Možemo! party proposed easier legal gender change and IVF inclusivity, but none of those bills had passed as of January 2024.

The blood transfusion institute's rules effectively bar gay and bisexual men from donating blood indefinitely: a 2007 bylaw places men who have sex with men under categories of permanent rejection, and as of 2021 this is framed as 'behaviors or activities that expose them to risk of contracting blood-borne infectious diseases'.

Pride events are documented in Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac and Pula, alongside the Balkans Trans Inter March. Community infrastructure includes three LGBT centres: the first in Zagreb, a second opened in Split on 24 May 2014 (run by association Risp-et, ahead of the 4th Split Pride on 7 June 2014, whose organisers demanded equal treatment of same-sex families), and a third in Rijeka on 16 October 2014 (LGBTIQ+ Druga Rijeka, publicly backed by mayor Vojko Obersnel). Zagreb has the largest scene, with clubs, bars and Queer Zagreb programming; gay-friendly venues and beaches are noted in Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik.

A European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Croatia (2024, reporting period 2023) assesses transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds.

In March 2014 Croatia granted asylum for the first time to a person persecuted on the basis of sexual orientation, a young man from Uganda who fled under the Uganda Anti-homosexuality Act. The sources say nothing about visa rules, passport gender markers, or entry procedures for transgender travellers.

In education, the European Committee on Social Rights found in 2009 discriminatory statements in a mandatory Croatian school biology textbook, ruling they violated the European Social Charter; on 1 March 2013 the Minister for Science, Education and Sports announced an action to strip homophobic content from elementary and high school books, especially religious education texts. A survey found 64% of Croatians agreed school lessons should include information about sexual orientation diversity and 63% about gender identity; a 2016 study on children in LGBT families found psychosocial adaptation alongside experiences of stigmatisation.
tangentialFactors:
An Intrepid Travel country guide states that Croatia 'widely accepts' LGBTQIA+ travellers but that public displays of affection may draw unwelcome responses in lesser-populated cities, and that gay venues are 'virtually non-existent outside Zagreb', now improving with new venues in Split, Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. This is visitor-facing nightlife and PDA guidance rather than a legal finding.

The 2018 Zagreb Pride report and the ILGA-Europe 2025 review document a pattern of under-reporting of homophobic and transphobic crime alongside escalating anti-gender disinformation, including a parliamentary session on 'Gender Ideology' without LGBTI organisation participation and disruption of the first Pula Pride march in 2024.

Youth and family support material includes Zagreb Pride's 2016 guide 'We Have a Family!' for LGBT parents and the 2018 picture book 'My Rainbow Family' for preschool-age children with same-sex parents (first 500 copies free, French Embassy funding; a crowdfunded reprint raised over $7,000). Partner-guardianship, granting permanent parental rights to a non-biological life partner, had its first case in July 2015.

outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not address visa rules, passport gender markers, or entry procedures for transgender travellers to Croatia; this remains unresolved in the record.

The European Commission 2024 country report on non-discrimination is cited only at the level of its subject matter (transposition and implementation of EU equality directives including SOGI grounds, reporting period 2023); specific findings are not detailed in the inventory and remain unresolved here.

The inventory provides no trans-specific violence figures for Croatia with denominators or comparison to general homicide rates, so no trans-specific violence magnitude can be stated.

The most recent documented incident of disruption against an LGBT event in the record is the disruption of the first Pula Pride march in 2024, covered by the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025; no later instance is documented.
